When the Black Death swept Europe
column2: From the late 1340s to the early 1350s the Black Death killed about one-quarter of Europeans, and the resulting labor shortage raised survivors' wages and access to land.

column1: When Zheng He's treasure fleet sailed
column2: Between 1405 and 1433 Ming China sent Zheng He on seven expeditions, with as many as 300 ships and 28,000 sailors, as far as eastern Africa.

column1: Where Europe stood in world commerce around 1450
column2: Around 1450 China dominated the world economy, while western Europe remained a poor, divided region on the edge of global trade.

column1: When Mehmet II conquered Constantinople
column2: In 1453 the Ottomans captured Constantinople, the Christian trading hub between Europe and Asia, deepening European fears for commerce and security.

column1: When European monarchs built stronger nation-states
column2: After 1450 Henry VII of England, Francis I of France, and Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain expanded royal power, gathering resources for armies, navies, and overseas ventures.

column1: When crusaders found sugar plantations
column2: After crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, Europeans took over its sugar plantations and adopted slave labor because sugar demanded relentless, cheap work.

column1: When sugar production moved to Mediterranean islands
column2: After Saladin reconquered Jerusalem in the twelfth century, European investors moved sugar plantations to eastern Mediterranean islands, starting sugar's westward march.

column1: When Portugal colonized the Atlantic islands
column2: In the late 1300s the Portuguese colonized the Canary Islands, and a few decades later Madeira and the Azores.

column1: When slave-worked sugar plantations reached the Atlantic islands
column2: By the early 1400s the Portuguese had established sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans on the Atlantic islands, a model for later American plantations.

column1: When the Portuguese met villagers on the Senegal River
column2: In 1455 Portuguese explorers met Senegal River villagers who were curious about European looks but were neither politically nor economically naive.

column1: When Columbus took his proposal to Spain
column2: In 1485, after nearly a decade of Portuguese rejection because experts judged his globe too small, Columbus left Portugal and appealed to Spain for support.

column1: When Bartolomeu Dias rounded Africa
column2: In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, proving that Portuguese ships could reach the Indian Ocean by sailing around Africa.

column1: When Vasco da Gama reached India
column2: In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India by sea, completing Portugal's direct route to Asian markets.

column1: When Spain completed the reconquista
column2: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella captured Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, freeing them to fund Columbus and further expansion.

column1: When Columbus first landed in the Americas
column2: On October 12, 1492, Columbus landed on San Salvador in the Bahamas, beginning lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

column1: When John Cabot reached North America
column2: In 1497 John Cabot, sailing for England, reached the coast near Newfoundland while seeking a northwest passage to Asia.

column1: When Spain imposed rule on the Caribbean
column2: From the 1490s to the early 1500s Spanish colonizers used warfare, forced labor, and mining against the Taino while Eurasian diseases sped their decline.

column1: When Cortés reached Mexico
column2: In 1519 Cortés landed on Mexico's Gulf Coast, learned of the Aztec Empire, and recruited its resentful enemies for an inland assault.

column1: When smallpox devastated central Mexico
column2: In 1520 and 1521 smallpox killed huge numbers of Aztecs, weakening resistance during Cortés's siege of Tenochtitlán.

column1: When Tenochtitlán surrendered
column2: In August 1521 Tenochtitlán fell to Cortés and his Indian allies, ending Aztec power and giving Spain control of Mexico.

column1: When Ponce de León was mortally wounded in Florida
column2: In 1521 Indians resisting Juan Ponce de León's Florida expedition mortally wounded him, ending his attempt to colonize Florida.

column1: When Pizarro conquered the Incas
column2: By 1532 Francisco Pizarro and his brothers had conquered the Inca Empire, extending Spanish rule into the silver-rich Andes of South America.

column1: When Coronado explored the Southwest
column2: Coronado's expedition entered the Southwest in 1539, reached the Grand Canyon and Great Plains, and returned to Mexico in 1542, when Crown officials tried him for great cruelties.

column1: When Spanish American silver production surged
column2: In the 1540s great silver strikes in Mexico and South America turned Spanish conquest into a large-scale capitalist mining enterprise.

column1: How large Potosí was by 1570
column2: By 1570 the silver-mining city of Potosí in the Andes held about 120,000 people, more than any city in Spain.

column1: How much silver Spanish America sent to Europe
column2: In the sixteenth century Spanish America shipped about 16,000 tons of silver to Europe, and the Spanish Crown claimed one-fifth of all silver mined.

column1: When Luther developed justification by faith
column2: Between 1513 and 1517 Martin Luther concluded that salvation was God's free gift received through faith, not a reward earned by good works.

column1: When Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses
column2: In 1517 Luther publicly attacked the sale of indulgences, turning criticism of Catholic abuses into a movement that challenged Church authority.

column1: When independent Lutheran churches formed
column2: In the 1520s Luther's followers organized their own churches in Germany, permanently breaking western Europe's Catholic unity.

column1: When Calvin published the Institutes of the Christian Religion
column2: In 1536 John Calvin published the Institutes of the Christian Religion, spreading his teachings on predestination and the calling across Europe.

column1: When the Huguenots first settled in America
column2: In 1562 Jean Ribault led French Huguenots to found a settlement on Parris Island, an early attempt at an American refuge that soon collapsed.

column1: When the Huguenots founded Fort Caroline
column2: In 1564 Huguenots built Fort Caroline in Florida and allied with the Timucua, alarming Spain about French piracy and expansion.

column1: When Spain founded St. Augustine
column2: In 1565 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine in Florida and destroyed Fort Caroline to block French Protestant expansion.

column1: When Gilbert received England's first colonial charter
column2: In 1578 Elizabeth I granted Humphrey Gilbert England's first charter to colonize America, but he died at sea before founding a settlement.

column1: When Raleigh launched the Roanoke project
column2: In 1584 Walter Raleigh received a royal patent, named the land Virginia, and sent settlers whose leaders soon alienated Wingina's people.

column1: When the second Roanoke colony arrived
column2: In 1587 John White brought 119 settlers, including families, to Roanoke, but supply shortages and Indian hostility soon left the colony vulnerable.

column1: When the Spanish Armada threatened England
column2: In 1588 Elizabeth kept every ship home to fight the Spanish Armada, delaying John White's return and stranding the Roanoke colonists.

column1: When John White found Roanoke deserted
column2: In 1590 John White returned to find Roanoke empty, with only the word CROATOAN carved on a post to hint at the colonists' fate.

column1: Where England stood in colonization by 1600
column2: By 1600, more than a century after Columbus, England still had no permanent American settlement, while Spain dominated most of the Americas.

column1: How Zheng He's junks compared with Columbus's ships
column2: Zheng He's largest junks were nine-masted and 400 feet long, while Columbus's largest 1492 ship was only 85 feet and all three ships carried about 90 men.

column1: When Cabot's second voyage vanished
column2: Cabot's second voyage sought a Northwest Passage to Asia, but his five ships disappeared in 1498.

column1: How many vessels fished Newfoundland by the 1550s
column2: By the 1550s about 400 vessels a year from England, France, Portugal, and Spain sailed to the Newfoundland fishery.

column1: Life expectancy and inequality in late-medieval Europe
column2: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries one-quarter of European children died in their first year, reaching 40 was fortunate, and nobles earned hundreds of times peasants' incomes.

column1: How deadly the Black Death was in cities
column2: The Black Death killed one-quarter of Europe's population and as much as 70 percent in some cities, provoking spiritual crisis and massacres of Jews.

column1: How many witches were executed in early modern Europe
column2: An estimated 40,000 to 60,000 accused witches were hanged or burned in early modern Europe, showing the lasting power of supernatural belief.

column1: How deadly malaria was for the Portuguese in West Africa
column2: Malaria killed roughly one-fourth to one-half of the Portuguese who tried to remain in West Africa, so Portugal partnered with coastal elites instead of conquering.

column1: Slavery's scale in the modern world
column2: Estimates cited in the chapter count up to 27 million people in labor bondage today and nearly 1 million sold across borders yearly.

column1: Africans in Lisbon by the mid-sixteenth century
column2: By the mid-sixteenth century people of African descent made up 10 percent of Lisbon's population.

column1: When Columbus arrived in Portugal
column2: Columbus was shipwrecked on Portugal's coast in 1476 and spent the next 10 years learning navigation and geography there.

column1: Spanish share of Spanish America's population by 1600
column2: By 1600 only about 5 percent of Spain's colonial population was Spanish-descended, and by 1800 only 300,000 Spanish immigrants had reached Central and South America.

column1: When African slaves were imported for West Indian sugar
column2: By 1520 large numbers of Black slaves were being imported from Africa to work Spain's West Indian sugar plantations.

column1: When Spain settled Georgia and Narváez invaded Florida
column2: Spain's 1526 settlement in present-day Georgia soon collapsed, and in 1528 Pánfilo de Narváez led 300 men into Florida.

column1: When Cabeza de Vaca reached Mexico City
column2: In July 1536 Spanish slavers found Cabeza de Vaca, Esteban, and two other castaways and brought the four survivors to Mexico City.

column1: How much French piracy cost Spain
column2: French attacks on Spanish galleons from 1556 to 1560 cut Spain's colonial revenue in half, motivating the destruction of Fort Caroline.

column1: How many Huguenots Menéndez killed
column2: In 1565 Menéndez attacked Fort Caroline with 500 soldiers and killed Jean Ribault and about 500 Huguenots in battle and executions.

column1: When Elizabeth began colonizing Ireland
column2: Beginning in 1565 Elizabeth I sponsored elite ventures to subdue Catholic Ireland and settle loyal English Protestants on Irish land.

column1: When Hakluyt wrote his Discourse
column2: In 1584 Richard Hakluyt wrote A Discourse Concerning Westerne Planting, urging Walter Raleigh's North American colonization.

column1: How Raleigh's second colony was organized
column2: Raleigh's second colony of 1587 recruited 119 men, women, and children, gave each a 500-acre estate, and made John White governor.

column1: When Drake rescued the first Roanoke colonists
column2: After Lane's men killed Wingina, Sir Francis Drake rescued 102 survivors of the first Roanoke colony.

column1: When the Stuart dynasty began
column2: Elizabeth I died in 1603, James I founded the Stuart dynasty, and in 1607 the English founded Jamestown on Chesapeake Bay.

column1: How long James I imprisoned Raleigh
column2: Walter Raleigh spent 15 years imprisoned by James I and was beheaded after a second defiance.

column1: How many de Soto's hogs numbered
column2: De Soto's pig herd sometimes exceeded 700, and hogs used over 80 percent of a carcass versus about 50 percent for cattle or sheep.

column1: When the Jesuit mission in Florida began
column2: In 1570 Menéndez encouraged a short-lived Jesuit mission as Spain added outposts across Florida.
